Senses.Explanation: In the central Chan use, having nothing to do means having no contrived spiritual business to pursue. Linji Yixuan calls the person with nothing to do noble, immediately says not to fabricate and simply to be ordinary, applies the designation to buddhas and patriarchs, and describes ordinary dressing, eating, and passing time. Huangbo Xiyun defines the person from two sides: feelings are exhausted with nothing left to depend on or grasp, and the person of the Way has no manifold mind. Sikongshan Benjing contrasts the Way's original absence of affairs with forcibly creating many affairs. Zhaozhou Congshen tells the community that those with a matter may discuss it while those without one should sit and investigate. Lan Can's song joins being naturally without affairs to nonalteration and warns against seeking work outside. The expression therefore denies fabricated pursuit, not attentive inquiry, ordinary activity, or responsive speech. Later independent records broaden the evidence: Yuanwu Keqin names an open field of nonaction and nothing-to-do, Dahui Zonggao says that when this is understood completely, function and substance need not be divided, while Yongjue Yuanxian dismisses the assembly with ‘nothing to do—return to the hall.’ These later uses confirm that the term can be asserted, qualified, and quoted rather than functioning only as an early Linji-school slogan.
Senses.Note: Eleven exact witnesses from seven distinct works now cover early formulas, ordinary activity, later quotation, criticism/inversion, investigation, and institutional address.

Senses.Explanation: A person with nothing going on is a named Chan person-label whose records both define and publicly test it. Guishan Lingyou says that when bad notions, feelings, views, imaginings, and habits are absent, one is like autumn water standing clear, clean, inactive, tranquil, and unobstructed: such a person is called a person of the Way and also a person with nothing going on. Baizhang Huaihai says that not being confused or disordered, angry or delighted at each object, and cleaning up at the gates of one's six faculties is being a person with nothing going on. Huangbo Xiyun says that when inner and outer feelings are dissolved and exhausted, with no dependence or grasping, this is a person with nothing going on. Linji Yixuan says that seeing as he has described leaves one a person with nothing going on for life. The record also supplies corrections: an unnamed guiding teacher quoted by Panshan Baoji says even an inactive person with nothing going on remains a difficult golden lock; Baoci Wensui quotes Fayan Wenyi saying that buddha is a person with nothing going on, then adds that such a person cannot now be found; and Muzhou Daoming invites such a person forward, only to send the approaching monk outside for twenty blows.
Senses.Note: The corpus has 253 matches in 109 files. Naming constructions have two matches in two files for 'called a person with nothing going on,' four in four for 'named,' and twenty-four in twenty-three for 'called.' 'Buddha is a person with nothing going on' occurs five times in five files; 'an inactive person with nothing going on' occurs seventy-six times in forty-three, and the corrective 'a person with nothing going on remains a difficult golden lock' occurs twice in two. The neighboring formula 'having nothing going on is the honored person' occurs six times in six files. The entry retains both the definitions and the record's explicit checks on adopting the label too quickly.

Senses.Explanation: Having no rank or assigned place in an ordered scheme. Chan turns that rank-language into a recurrent predicate and name. Linji's best-known deployment is the 'true person without rank,' said to be on the lump of red flesh and to go in and out through people's face-gates. The bare term functions as an answer: asked 'how is it?' Guanxi says 'without rank'; when challenged whether that is the same as empty space, he replies 'you butcher.' Elsewhere an unnamed monk asks why the figure identified as teacher has no rank/order; the answer says ancient and present cannot arrange it and the three times cannot place it. A rank-system exchange asks, 'when merit is turned and there is no rank, how is it?' and receives 'the royal house's affairs are manifest.' Another address contrasts name and rank with no rank and no name. The Zen deviation is this removal of ordered rank from a public figure, answer, spatial ordering, and formal rank-system question. The standalone entry records that family while leaving Linji's full figure in its own article.

Senses.Explanation: The true person of no rank is Linji Yixuan's figure for what he says constantly goes in and out through each person's face. Later records repeatedly raise, question, verse, criticize, and reinterpret that formulation. Xitai Bian explicitly raises Linji's phrase and rejects both the dried-shit-stick retort and easy appropriation. Gulin Qingmao depicts the figure as difficult to distinguish while manifesting at the crown and in the eyes. Shanfeng Xian lists it as Linji's signature expression beside other teachers' stock responses. The Yongzheng Emperor says the rankless designation is itself only a forced name and plays rank against no-rank. Caoyuan Sheng scolds Linji for calling it a true person of no rank. These conflicting deployments preserve one Linji-derived figure without licensing one uniform later explanation.

Senses.Explanation: Not dwelling or not abiding names the phrase's relational sense. The raw headword occurs 1,252 times in 239 allowed texts; that total includes both the phrase and the personal name Wuzhu. Huineng gives the fullest direct description of the phrase: 'Not dwelling is people's original nature' (無住者，人之本性). He continues through good and bad, beautiful and ugly, hostile and friendly, and verbal conflict, saying not to think of former objects from thought to thought. He then names the contrast: if former, present, and later thoughts continue without break, this is called binding; 'from thought to thought, not dwelling on all things is no binding—this is taking not-dwelling as the root' (於諸法上念念不住，即無縛也。此是以無住為本). Fayan's recorded case begins from the line 'from the root of not-dwelling establish all things'; asked what that root is, Fayan answers, 'form arises before substance; name arises before naming' (形興未質，名起未名). Wansong's case commentary preserves another explicit exchange: asked what the root of not-dwelling rests on, the answer is 'not-dwelling has no root' (無住則無本). In the Shenhui and Huineng encounter, Shenhui says, 'Take not-dwelling as the root; seeing is the host' (以無住為本。見即是主). Later records pair 'not-dwelling as root' with 'no-thought as source' and call the root of not-dwelling the root of all things. The recurring grammar is verbal and relational: thoughts do not dwell, a root does not itself rest on another root, and things are said to be established from it.
Senses.Note: The direct Huineng definition, the Fayan public case, Shenhui's reply, and later comments are retained as distinct witnesses. 'Without a place to dwell' (dwelling nowhere) occurs 370 times in 145 texts; 'not-dwelling as the root' (無住為本) occurs 44 times in 27; 'root of not-dwelling' (無住本) occurs 135 times in 64; and 'not-dwelling mind' (the non-abiding mind) occurs 38 times in 30. Biographical occurrences where these two graphs form the name Wuzhu were excluded from semantic evidence.

SearchAliases: person of the Way with no reliance
Senses.Explanation: Linji’s “person of the Way with no reliance” names the presently hearing person in his hall addresses, which call that person the mother of buddhas and the one who rides circumstances. Literally, a person of the Way with no reliance . Linji repeatedly identifies this figure with the person presently listening to the teaching: 'the person of the Way with no reliance who is listening to the teaching right now' , plainly distinct and never lacking. He calls this person 'the mother of the buddhas' , says buddhas are born from no reliance, and says buddha-settings cannot name themselves—the person with no reliance rides the setting and comes out. He further says that although this person is the leaky substance of the five aggregates, it is earth-walking spiritual power, and that moving and not moving are two settings used by this person. The Zen bend is Linji's relocation of an apparently wandering ascetic title into the live teaching assembly: it names the hearer before him and the invariant person that uses changing named settings. Later records overwhelmingly quote, explain, challenge, and even warn against holding to this Linji formula; this distinct formulation therefore remains master-keyed.

Senses.Explanation: A holeless iron hammer is a solid, unusable hammer-head image; separately, the phrase can be applied as a label to a person. An impossible solid hammer-head with no eye through which a handle could be fitted; the phrase calls this imagined object ‘iron,’ but does not document an actual manufactured tool. The phrase occurs 256 times in 108 allowlisted texts. Chan records repeatedly deploy this unusable hammer as an image of something offering no point of entry. Fachang Yiyu says that water cannot wet it and wind cannot enter it, ‘like a holeless iron hammer’ (水灑不著。風吹不入。如箇無孔鐵鎚相似). Huguo Cian Jingyuan gives it as the direct answer to ‘What thing can heaven not cover and earth not support?’ Xuedou Chongxian's verse speaks of ‘a holeless iron hammer driving in a wedge again’ (無孔鐵鎚重下楔), and Yuanweng Xin calls the whole ten-direction world such a hammer while denying any place for conjecture. These are deployments of the solid object-image, distinct from passages that directly call people holeless iron hammers.

Senses.Explanation: The phrase names Zhaozhou Congshen's single answer “no” taken up as the object of inquiry, not bare negation or wordlessness. Wumen Huikai calls this one word the single barrier of the school and instructs readers to raise a mass of doubt and investigate it day and night, explicitly rejecting both nihilistic void and ordinary has-versus-has-not interpretation. Dahui Zonggao calls the one word a knife cutting off the road of life and death and repeatedly tells readers simply to raise it rather than manufacture interpretive ideas. Gaofeng Yuanmiao reports keeping watch on it for nearly three years. Xueyan Zuqin describes raising the word lightly at the nose when miscellaneous thoughts arise and putting it down again when they cease. Zhongfeng Mingben asks why Zhaozhou said this word and directs attention firmly to the saying while raising great doubt. The corpus defines the item through the dog case, named barrier, repeated raising, and explicit rejection of ordinary negation.

Senses.Explanation: As a named condition, “no-mind” does not mean inert unconsciousness. Huangbo Xiyun directly says that no-mind is having no mind of any kind, calls it the way, and warns that deliberately using mind to make mind absent turns mind into something present. Dahui Zonggao explicitly excludes being insensate like earth, wood, tiles, or stones; he describes meeting objects and conditions without fixation, attachment, obstruction, or residence even in purity, and distinguishes this from merely saying “no-mind.” Sikong Benjing argues for “no-mind is the way” while interlocutors test whether mindless rubble would then count. Luopu Yuanan and Falan Yuancheng preserve the named “person of no-mind” in questions, while Yulin Tongxiu warns that even no-mind remains separated by a barrier. The term is thus affirmative, defined, tested, and criticized across the corpus rather than a simple command to suppress thought.

Senses.Explanation: In ordinary adverbial syntax, the headword means acting without intending the result. Senses.Explanation: No-thought is defined as functioning amid thought without fixation, not forcibly blanking the mind. Huineng places it beside no-form and no-abiding and defines it as being amid thought without thought. He says seeing all things without the mind becoming stained is no-thought, while thinking of nothing and cutting thought off is bondage and a one-sided view. He also warns that eliminating a single thought is death. The Dunhuang recension independently defines no-thought as seeing all things while sticking to none. Huineng's character-by-character explanation says what is absent is dual marks and the dust-and-toil mind, while what is thought of is true-thus original nature. Shenhui answers that the no-thought teaching is asserted as neither existent nor nonexistent. Nanyue Jiqi quotes a threefold formula linking realization of no-thought with penetrating things and seeing the awakened ones' realm. These are explicit textual boundaries against a blank-mind gloss.

Senses.Explanation: No arising is the claim that things do not come into birth or arise. Chan records make it something to embody, awaken to, realize, and question, but they also refuse to identify it with dormant stillness or a secure place in which to settle. Yongjue Yuanxian gives the sharpest direct boundary. He rejects calling ‘the mechanism quiescent and not yet issuing forth’ no arising (指機寂未發謂之無生), then says that things do not arise from themselves, from another, jointly, or without a cause; when none of these four modes arises, there truly is no arising (諸法不自生，不他生，不共生，不無因生，四俱不生，則實無生). In the Yongjia encounter, Huineng asks why Yongjia Xuanjue does not embody no arising and comprehend what has no speed; Yongjia answers that embodiment itself is no arising and comprehension originally has no speed (何以體取無生，了無速乎；體即無生，了本無速). The Visvabhu Buddha section of the Compendium of the Five Lamps attributes a verse saying that mind is originally without arising but exists because of objects (心本無生因境有). Guxue Zhe asks for ‘a phrase of no arising’ (如何是無生底句), Foyin Zhiqing says one can realize it immediately and then asks the assembly whether they want to see it, Puan Yinsu says that once it is awakened to it is never mistaken, and Konggu Daocheng asks for its meaning before comparing it to vast empty space. Chushi Fanqi supplies the strongest recorded reversal: when the mind dwells in no arising, no arising itself is birth and death; he raises the staff and says, ‘this is not no arising’ (心住，無生即生死；拈拄杖，云：這箇不是無生). Longer phrases preserve the base wording but add their own lexical work. Yang Jie criticizes further talk of no arising (更說無生話); Huineng pairs no arising with no extinguishing (無生無滅); Liangshan Yuanguan banishes recognition into ‘the country of no arising’ and then calls that resting place dead water that holds no dragon; Chushi cites ‘endurance concerning no arising beneath the staff’ (棒下無生忍); and Guifeng Zongmi explicitly names the longer phrase ‘endurance concerning no arising’ (無生法忍). These families show how Chan loads and tests the words without turning every compound into evidence for a second bare-headword sense.

Senses.Explanation: Without marks, or markless, is a phrase for being apart from marks, appearance, or form. It is attested within 2,588 total occurrences across 324 allowlisted texts. Huineng's Platform Record gives a direct definition: "markless means being among marks while apart from marks" (無相者，於相而離相). It also says the teaching establishes "marklessness as its body" (無相為體, 11 occurrences). A later small assembly quotes that three-part formula and asks why marklessness is not also made the source. In a Compendium encounter, an unnamed questioner asks, "what is without marks?" and Layman Pangyun answers, "mountains green, waters verdant" (如何是無相；山青水綠). Transmission wording places "true form, markless" (實相無相, 103) between "the subtle mind of extinction" and "subtle correct teaching." The corpus further records Mazu Daoyi asking how to accord with "markless complete command" (無相三昧). These definitions, questions, compounds, and quotations keep the phrase tied to marks and their absence; this entry does not turn it into an imported theory.

Senses.Explanation: To bind oneself without a rope is to create one’s own confinement where no external restraint exists; particular passages locate that self-binding in a phrase, side, or position. One source places the phrase after “the second sentence,” Lingyin Li applies it to Bodhidharma after Emperor Wu presses him, and Liao’an Qingyu uses it for failing to pass through. Chaozong’s fox discussion asks whether discarding “not falling into causation” and guarding “not obscuring causation” would itself be binding oneself without a rope; that same passage keeps causation in view. A frozen concordance audit records 287 hits across 145 works, with seven broad karma-family proximity hits inside sixty characters and 280 without them. Those counts describe lexical proximity, not sense, so they support only the restrained conclusion that the phrase is not a karma term by default.
